title: Assemble a rack-and-pinion parallel gripper so both fingers open evenly
keywords: bimanual, rack and pinion, parallel gripper, gear mesh, tooth phase, robot assembly, mechatronics technician, gripper repair, mesh two racks, symmetric jaws, precision seating
instruction: Assemble the gripper: seat the loose white rack on the pinion so both fingers open evenly about the centre, then let go.
context: Mechatronics technicians and robot assemblers (O*NET 17-3024.00 Electro-Mechanical and Mechatronics Technologists and Technicians) rebuild the parallel-jaw grippers that robot arms use, a rack on each side of one pinion. The second rack must drop in at the same tooth phase as the first, or the jaws sit off-centre and every grasp an arm then learns on that hardware is biased. Seating the rack so the jaws open evenly is the hands-on step that decides how well robot hardware can be built and trusted for learning.
setup: Station table; world metres from the midpoint between the two arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left, z up; table top z 0.7475. All parts are real size, within the arms' 0.35 m reach, 50 N finger force and 94 mm jaw opening. (1) Gripper housing: grey ABS, 52 x 160 x 4 mm floor plate with two 3.5 x 150 x 12 mm outer walls whose inner faces are 45 mm apart, two 4 x 4 x 12 mm steel stop blocks, 1.0 kg, fixed, centre (0.12, 0.0), long side along y. (2) Pinion: stainless steel, hub 14 mm diameter by 12 mm tall, eight 3 mm dowel pins on a 24 mm pitch circle (module 3), 40 g, free to turn on a vertical shaft at the housing centre, friction under 0.002 N m; starts turned one tooth (45 deg). (3) Near rack: white powder-coated steel, 72 mm long, 11.75 mm wide, 12 mm tall, eight 2 mm teeth at 9.42 mm pitch, 60 g, with a bridge and a 6 mm finger plate (23 and 40 mm above the floor) at its leading end and a 7 x 6 x 19.5 mm handle post over its tail tooth; in its channel at pitch line x 0.108, 0.75 mm clear of the wall, started 9.42 mm open (jaw opening is measured from its stop). (4) Far rack: identical, mirrored, 60 g, white, lying on a 70 x 115 x 4 mm dark grey feed tray (0.3 kg, fixed) at (0.172, 0.065), the far rack's pitch line at x 0.172 and its centre at y 0.058; its channel is the housing's far one (pitch line x 0.132). Both racks slide on the floor (friction about 0.25); the two stop blocks hold both closed.
scoring: Measured from both racks' poses every control step; s_N, s_F are the finger plates' travel (mm) from their stops, d = (s_N - s_F)/2. A rack is seated when its pitch line is within 2 mm of its channel, its centre within 1.5 mm of the floor-seated height, within 3 deg of level and 4 deg of straight. 0: either rack not seated (a rack lifted out and set beside the housing is not), or the near rack alone never drove the far rack open 15 mm (opening travel counted only while both racks are seated and no gripper is within 5 mm of the far rack). 0.25: |d| above 3.0 mm. 0.5: |d| at most 3.0 mm, jaws under 15 mm each. 0.75: s_N and s_F at least 15 mm. 1.0: 0.75, both racks still (under 3 mm/s) for 1 s and both grippers' pad points at least 30 mm from the housing and racks, moving under 5 mm/s, for 1 s (success must hold 1 s). Only the final state counts; a wrong try that is undone costs nothing. Real trial: a 1 mm tape scale along each finger plate's path with the housing centre line marked gives s_N, s_F, d; a straightedge across the pinion and a feeler at each rack's walls check seating; the video shows which hand touches which rack during the pull.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Slide the near rack to 9.42 mm open (one tooth) with its stop side toward you; turn the pinion until a pin sits in a tooth gap of the near rack; lay the far rack on the tray at the marked spot, tail toward the left arm, finger plate toward the centre. Check: the pinion turns under 3 gf at a 100 mm arm, each rack slides under 20 gf on a spring scale, and the rack-to-wall clearance passes a 0.5 mm feeler and fails a 1.0 mm one.
fidelity: Rack teeth are 2 mm thick straight-flank and the pinion has pins (a pin-rack approximation of module-3 gearing) so the mesh is robust at 20 Hz; real teeth are involute and thicker, with less backlash. Masses are rounded. The floor is a smooth plate and the racks have no cover; a real gripper has a cover and bearings. The demo needs the arm's sag corrected from the seen pose to 0.5 mm.
